questions.stem: A 72-year-old man presented after a syncopal episode associated with firing of his implanted cardioverter-defibrillator (AICD). He had also had a 4-week history of fever and chills. He had undergone an AICD exchange 2 months earlier. He had a history of coronary artery disease and prior CABG, congestive heart failure, and had had an AICD for 15 years. On examination his temperature was 38.4°C, heart rate was 105 beats/min, blood pressure was 110/80 mmHg, O2 saturation 98% on room air. His AICD site had a wellhealed incision with no erosion or discharge, but there was fluctuance over the AICD pocket. He was started on vancomycin. Investigations: Total white cell count 15,000/mm3 Blood cultures: gram-positive cocci in clusters seen
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding echocardiogram?

options.text: Delayed transthoracic echocardiogram after AICD removal
No need for transthoracic echocardiogram as it will not change management because AICD needs to be removed anyway
Urgent transthoracic echocardiogram and if negative, OK to retain AICD generator and leads
Urgent transthoracic echocardiogram but AICD will require removal independent of results

questions.explanation: Urgent transthoracic echocardiogram, but AICD will require removal independent of results This patient is presenting with sepsis and an occult source of bacteremia in the setting of a recent AICD exchange. This is a common presentation for cardiac implanted electronic device-related infection. Whenever a device-related infection is suspected in a bacteremic patient, the next step in evaluation would be to obtain an echocardiogram to evaluate for the presence of valvular or wire-related endocarditis. Although the absence of vegetations on echocardiogram would not preclude the need for removal of the device, it would potentially affect the duration of antimicrobial therapy, need for valvular surgery, and timing to re-implantation of the device. Even if the transthoracic echocardiogram is negative, the patient has evidence of device infection. In this setting device removal is always recommended due to the high rates of relapsed infection with device retention. Even though it is true that the device should be removed independent of the echo results, these can affect the duration of antimicrobial therapy, need for valvular surgery, and time to re-implantation of the device. Transesophageal echocardiogram is incorrect because the right-sided chambers are actually in the anterior portion of the heart. Therefore the distance traveled by ultrasound waves in a thin patient can be shorter than those from a transesophageal approach. As a result, the images can be just as good if not better, obviating the need for a transesophageal echocardiogram in all patients.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q16

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman presented with subjective fevers without any localizing symptoms or signs. She had received a left ventricular assist device 6 months ago as destination strategy for chemotherapy-induced nonischemic cardiomyopathy on a background of breast cancer. On examination, her temperature was 101.4°F (38.5°C), her heart rate was 100 beats/minute, and her blood pressure was 136/80 mmHg. Investigations: 4/4 blood cultures positive for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, resistant only to penicillin on extended susceptibility testing (sensitive to oxacillin, ceftriaxone, cefazolin, vancomycin, TMP– SMX, doxycycline, and clindamycin) CT chest/abdomen/pelvis: a large fluid collection surrounding the VAD pump with associated stranding and enhancement Aspirate of collection fluid: MSSA isolated She was deemed to be a poor candidate for open debridement and washout, and nor was she a candidate for pump exchange.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Cefazolin For deep LVAD infections, especially with associated bacteremia with an aggressive organism such as MSSA, it is best to initiate treatment with an IV agent with cidal activity for at least 6 weeks followed by suppression with an oral agent. This is done due to concern for biofilm formation and the inability to control the source of the infection. Vancomycin, daptomycin, dalbavancin, and linezolid should not be used first-line for MSSA infection.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q17

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presented with increased erythema, drainage, and tenderness around the driveline to a left ventricular assist device (LVAD). He had nonischemic cardiomyopathy and was awaiting heart transplantation. Investigations: Ultrasound of the exit site: small fluid collection at the site The expressed drainage was sent for culture.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Coagulase-negative staphylococci Approximately 50% of all LVAD and MCS (mechanical circulatory support) infections are due to gram-positive organisms including coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, and enterococcal species. In the case of driveline infections, these are more likely to be introduced as ascending infection from the exit site in the abdomen. Although Enterobacteriaceae and Pseudomonas are important causes of infection, these are not epidemiologically more likely than gram-positive infections. Cutibacterium can be seen as a cause of infection in MCS, especially in pacers and AICD infections, but these are not close in frequency to staphylococcal infections. Candida species are found only rarely to be associated with driveline infections.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q7

questions.question: ICD pocket infection 15 month post and has 3 weeks of pocket site issues and patient well – beyond blood cultures what other 2 tests would you do prior while awaiting removal?

parts.text: Beyond blood cultures what other 2 tests would you do prior while awaiting removal?
There is no pus from the dehisced wound and patient has received cephalexin x 1 week prior to this.  If all tests were negative how long would you treat post removal?

cohort_answer.text:
Tests: ECG, echocardiogram, pacemaker pocket culture (if going to surgeon)
Duration if all negative: 2 weeks

questions.question: 12) man, 50s, ICD 15mos ago. Recent incisional opening, no pus.

parts.text: a) what 2 tests would you do aside from blood cultures?
b) What is the most likely aerobic bug?
c) What is the most likely anaerobic bug?
d) If all tests negative, duration of treatment?

cohort_answer.text: Tests: Swab of pocket and device; TTE/TEE. Most likely aerobic bug: Coagulase negative staphylococci. Most likely anaerobic bug: C. acnes. Duration: 10 days (pocket erosion) or 2 weeks (pocket infection)

parts.text: Name 4 infections associated with them.
Why do they make bacteria resistant to killing?

cohort_answer.text: Infections: PJI, IE, Vascular graft infections, diabetic foot infections and dental caries, CF infections. Resistance: Significantly increases the effective MIC by preventing adequate delivery of antibiotic to the organism.

questions.question: Someone had ICD placed 15 mos ago, generator eroded through skin, cardiologist did not see any pus.

parts.text: What are 2 investigations other than blood cultures to help with diagnosis?
What is most common aerobic GPC? What is most common anaerobe?
After explanation what duration would you treat for?

questions.model_answer:
a) Two investigations (besides blood cultures): (1) transesophageal echocardiography to assess for lead vegetation/associated endocarditis (2) culture and Gram stain of the device pocket tissue/generator at the time of extraction (18F-FDG PET/CT is another useful adjunct for occult device infection).
b) Most common aerobic gram-positive coccus: coagulase-negative staphylococci (Staphylococcus epidermidis). Most common anaerobe: Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes).
c) Duration of antibiotics after complete device (generator and lead) extraction: 10-14 days if blood cultures clear promptly and there is no associated endocarditis/lead vegetation; 4-6 weeks if there is associated valvular or lead endocarditis or persistent bacteremia.

questions.question: Someone had ICD placed 15 months ago, generator eroded through skin. Cardiologist did not see any pus.

parts.text: A) What are 2 investigations other than BCx to help with dx?
B) What is the most common aerobic GPC?
C) What is the most common anaerobe?
D) After explanation what duration would you tx for?

cohort_answer.text:
TEE; Culture from ICD pocket
CNST
C. acnes
Depends.. If BCx and TEE negative, as per AHA 7-10 days vs HRS/IDSA 14 days. "When CIED infection is limited to the pocket site, 7 to 10 days of therapy after device removal is reasonable if the presentation is device erosion without inflammatory changes; otherwise, 10 to 14 days of antimicrobial treatment is recommended." - AHA

parts.text: A) Name 4 situations where there can be biofilm formation, not involving prosthetic material?

cohort_answer.text: Infective endocarditis; Wound infections; Cystic fibrosis; Otitis media; Oral cavity/dental caries, periodontitis; Chronic bacterial prostatitis (speaker notes: CF, PICC Line, endocarditis, pseudo)

parts.text: B) Name 2 features of biofilms that reduce the efficacy of abx?

cohort_answer.text: Large extracellular matrix so abx cannot penetrate; Easier transfer of resistance genes within biofilm; Stationary growth phase of some bacteria within biofilm so beta lactams have less effect; Altered microenvironment (pH, O2, CO2) that impairs effect of some abx; Presence of "persisters" - non-dividing, more resistant organisms; Inoculum effect and drug penetration (speaker notes: thick cell wall, LPS; extracellular matrix)

parts.text: C) Give 2 reasons that rifampin can improve the chances of antimicrobial therapy succeeding?

cohort_answer.text: Active against metabolically dormant bacteria; able to penetrate S. epidermidis biofilm and can prevent biofilm formation within minutes. In vitro, addition of rifampin to S. epidermidis and MRSA biofilm infections improved susceptibility to other antibiotics and decreased adherence of bacteria to foreign material

parts.text: D) When can you use RIF alone?

cohort_answer.text: Latent TB; Chemoprophylaxis for invasive meningococcal disease exposure; Eradicate pharyngeal carriage of group B streptococci in infants with recurrent GBS sepsis

parts.text: E) Define quorum sensing

cohort_answer.text: Complex mechanism of circulating molecules and "signals" within the biofilm matrix allowing organisms to "communicate" to help regulate biofilm formation. Enables bacteria to restrict expression of specific genes to high cell densities at which resulting phenotypes will be most beneficial. Common phenotypes: biofilm formation, virulence factor expression, motility

questions.question: 4. Man has mycobacteria chimera infection due to heart transplant.

parts.text: a) What device is implicated in this?
b) The device is in your hospital but cannot be removed. What are two things you could do, intra-operatively, to reduce transmission of this infection?
c) This man comes in for investigations. What isolation precautions should he be under?

cohort_answer.text: Device: contaminated heater-cooler devices (Stockert 3T, LivaNova PLC). Intra-op measures: ensure maintenance of laminar flow in OR to not disrupt positive pressure; have air/water filters installed in heater coolers to filter bacteria; reduce aerosolization of water tank via tight sealing and directing fan away from procedure. Isolation: No precautions needed - standard
